## Chapter Overview {.center}

- Precise knowledge of liver, biliary tract, and pancreas architecture is essential for HPB surgery
- Covers gross anatomy, functional/segmental anatomy, vascular anatomy, biliary anatomy, and common anatomic variants
- Integrates classic descriptions (Couinaud, Healey & Schroy, Bismuth) with the Brisbane 2000 terminology
- Heavy emphasis on radiologic correlation (US, CT, MRI/MRCP, angiography, cholangiography)

## Section 1: The Liver — Gross Anatomy

## Liver — Position and Relations

- Lies protected under the lower ribs, applied to the diaphragm, sitting on the IVC posteriorly
- Most bulk is **right of midline**; lower border near the right costal margin
- Extends as a wedge **left of midline**, between the stomach and the left hemidiaphragm
- Upper surface convex, molded to diaphragm
- Surface projection: up to the **4th intercostal space** (right) and **5th intercostal space** (left)

## Liver — Peritoneal Coverings

- Invested by peritoneum **except** the posterior "bare area"
- Peritoneum reflects onto the diaphragm → forms **right and left triangular ligaments**
- Undersurface concave, ending at a sharp anterior border
- Posterior surface triangular, base to the right — the **bare area** lies between upper and lower leaves of the triangular ligament
- Peritoneum reflects from Gerota's fascia onto the right posterior liver; **right adrenal gland** lies beneath this reflection
- Anteriorly attached to diaphragm by falciform ligament, left triangular ligament, and upper layer of right triangular ligament

## Figure 2.1 — Posterior Aspect (C)

- IVC sits snugly in a deep groove within the bare area; hepatic veins open directly into it
- **Right suprarenal gland** lies adjacent to IVC within the bare area; adrenal vein drains into the right of the IVC
- **Caudate lobe** slopes from inferior to posterior surface, demarcated on the left by a fissure containing the **ligamentum venosum**
- Gastrohepatic omentum attaches to the ligamentum venosum → places caudate lobe within the **lesser sac**
- Left lobe's posterior surface is narrow with a fine bare area

## Figure 2.1 — The Ligament of the Vena Cava

- A fibrous layer passes from the posterior liver edge toward the lumbar vertebrae, fanning out posteriorly (especially superiorly)
- Behind the IVC, it joins a fibrous extension from the caudate lobe's lateral edge
- Called the **ligament of the vena cava**
- Must be divided:
  - **Right side** → exposes IVC and right hepatic vein
  - **Left side** → mobilizes the caudate lobe
- Occasionally liver tissue completely embraces the IVC (tunnel of parenchyma)

## Retrohepatic Inferior Vena Cava

- IVC runs to the **right of the aorta**, diverging from it as it ascends
- Below the liver: lies behind duodenum and pancreatic head (retroperitoneal)
- Passes upward behind the **foramen of Winslow**, posterior to right hilar structures
- **Renal veins** lie anterior to the renal arteries, joining IVC at near-right angle (left) and obliquely (right)
- IVC embraced in a groove on the posterior liver surface

## IVC — Course Through the Diaphragm

- IVC lies on the right crus of the diaphragm, behind the bare area
- Extends to the **central tendon of the diaphragm**, pierced at the level of **T8**
- This is behind and higher than the origin of the abdominal aorta
- Separated from the right crus by:
  - The **right celiac ganglion** (lower)
  - The **right phrenic artery** (higher)

## IVC — Tributaries

- **Right adrenal vein**: short vessel entering IVC behind the bare area
  - Occasional small **accessory right adrenal vein** → enters confluence of right renal vein and IVC
  - Occasionally drains directly into the posterior liver
- **Lumbar veins**: drain posterolaterally into the IVC **below** the renal vein level
- **Above** the renal vein level: usually no posterior vena caval tributaries

## Hepatic Veins — Overview (Figs 2.2–2.4)

- Drain the **upper posterior surface** of the liver at an oblique angle directly into the IVC
- **Right hepatic vein (RHV)**: largest; short extrahepatic course (~1–2 cm)
- **Left (LHV) and Middle (MHV) hepatic veins**:
  - May drain separately into IVC
  - Usually join to form a common venous channel (~2 cm) → enters left anterior IVC surface below diaphragm

## Hepatic Veins — Umbilical Vein & Accessory Veins

- **Umbilical vein** (of the liver, NOT the fetal umbilical vein):
  - Single in most patients
  - Runs beneath the falciform ligament between MHV and LHV
  - Empties into the terminal LHV (rarely into MHV or the MHV–LHV confluence)
- **Accessory right hepatic vein**: present inferiorly in ~**15%** of patients (see Fig 2.3)
- **Caudate lobe**: drains **directly into the IVC** (unique among segments)

## Figure 2.2 — Ultrasound of Hepatic Vein Confluence

- Transverse ultrasound image
- Demonstrates the **Left (L)**, **Middle (M)**, and **Right (R)** hepatic veins
- All three converge and join the **IVC**
- Classic sonographic landmark for confirming hepatic venous anatomy before resection

## Figure 2.4 — Major Extrahepatic Veins and Falciform Ligament

- Anterior surfaces of major extrahepatic veins and the IVC are **retroperitoneal**
- These are **masked behind the layers of the falciform ligament** as it splits toward the right and left triangular ligaments
- Note: LHV and MHV usually join **within** the liver — depicted as joining outside the liver here only for visual simplicity

## Section 2: Functional Surgical Anatomy

## Functional Anatomy — Historical Foundations

- Internal architecture = segments combining into **sectors**, separated by scissurae containing hepatic veins (Fig 2.5)
- Key historical contributors:
  - **McIndoe & Counseller (1927)** — bilaterality of the liver
  - **Hjörtsjö (1931)** — intrahepatic duct topography
  - **Ton That Tung (1939, 1979)** — hepatic venous vascularization & resections
  - **Healey & Schroy (1953)** — biliary duct anatomy/branching patterns
  - **Goldsmith & Woodburne (1957)** — surgical anatomy for liver resection
  - **Couinaud (1957)** — definitive segmental nomenclature
  - **Bismuth et al. (1982)** — major/minor "réglée" segmentectomies

## Four Sectors and the Main Portal Scissura

- Three main hepatic veins (within scissurae) divide the liver into **four sectors**, each receiving its own portal pedicle
- **Main portal scissura**:
  - Contains the **middle hepatic vein**
  - Runs from the middle of the gallbladder bed (anterior) to the left of the IVC (posterior)
- Right and left livers (demarcated by the main portal scissura) are **independent** in portal/arterial vascularization and biliary drainage (Fig 2.6)
- Each hemiliver is further divided into two by the remaining portal scissurae

## Goldsmith/Woodburne "Segments" vs. Couinaud "Sectors"

| Term | Author | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| **Segments** | Goldsmith & Woodburne (1957) | The 4 major subdivisions of right & left liver |
| **Sectors** | Couinaud (1957) | Same 4 subdivisions, different name |

- Important: terminology overlap is a frequent source of confusion across textbooks

## Right Portal Scissura

- Separates the **right liver** into two sectors:
  - **Anteromedial (anterior)**
  - **Posterolateral (posterior)**
- With the body supine, this scissura is almost in the **frontal plane**
- The **right hepatic vein** runs within the right scissura

## Left Portal Scissura

- Divides the **left liver** into two sectors
- **Important distinction**: the left portal scissura is **NOT** within the umbilical fissure
  - The umbilical fissure is **not a portal scissura** — it contains a portal pedicle instead
- The left portal scissura lies **posterior to the ligamentum teres**, within the left liver, along the course of the **left hepatic vein**

## Brisbane 2000 Terminology — Transition

- Couinaud's terminology widely used, but being replaced by the **International Hepato-Pancreatico-Biliary Association (2000)** alternative
- Main difference: Couinaud's **"sectors"** → renamed **"sections"**
- Left medial *section* (Strasberg, 2005) = **one segment only** (Segment IV)

## Table 2.1 — Brisbane Terminology of Liver Anatomy and Resections

| Anatomic Term | Couinaud Segments | Surgical Resection |
|---|---|---|
| Right hemiliver / right liver | 5–8 | Right hepatectomy |
| Left hemiliver / left liver | 2–4 | Left hepatectomy |
| Right anterior section | 5, 8 | Right anterior sectionectomy |
| Right posterior section | 6, 7 | Right posterior sectionectomy |
| Left medial section | 4 | Left medial sectionectomy / Resection of segment 4 |
| Left lateral section | 2, 3 | Left lateral sectionectomy / Bisectionectomy 2,3 |
| — | 4,5,6,7,8 | Right trisectionectomy / Extended right hepatectomy |
| — | 2,3,4,5,8 | Left trisectionectomy / Extended left hepatectomy |

## Figure 2.5 — Portal Triad Distribution

- Portal vein, hepatic artery, and bile ducts distributed in a **symmetric pedicular pattern**
- This belies the **asymmetric** external appearance of the liver
- Each segment (**I–VIII**) supplied by a portal triad (portal vein + hepatic artery branch) and drained by a tributary of right/left hepatic ducts
- **Portal sectors** (= "sections" in Brisbane terminology) = parenchyma supplied by independent portal pedicles
- **Hepatic scissurae** = scissurae containing the portal pedicles
- The umbilical fissure corresponds to a hepatic scissura

## Figure 2.5 — Right and Left "Liver" vs. "Lobe"

- Internal architecture = **two hemilivers**, separated by the **main portal scissura** (a.k.a. **Cantlie's line**)
- Preferred terminology: **right and left liver** (NOT "right and left lobes")
- "Lobes" is erroneous — there is **no visible external mark** that identifies a true hemiliver
- Right scissura → right hepatic vein
- Main scissura → middle hepatic vein
- Left scissura → left hepatic vein

## Figure 2.6 — Couinaud's Segmental Map (A & B)

- Functional division of the liver into segments **I through VIII** per Couinaud's nomenclature
- **A**: As seen in the patient (in situ orientation)
- **B**: Ex vivo position
- Segments arranged around the portal pedicle distribution and the three hepatic veins
- Forms the conceptual basis for all segment-oriented resections

## Section 3: Hilar Portal Vein Branching

## Portal Triad at the Hilum

- Right portal triad: short course (~**1–1.5 cm**) before entering right liver substance (Fig 2.7)
- In some cases, right anterior and posterior pedicles arise **independently**, separated by up to **2 cm**
- In some cases, the **left portal vein appears to arise from the right anterior branch** (trifurcation pattern — see Fig 2.40)

## Left Portal Pedicle — The Umbilical Fissure Course

- On the left side, the portal triad crosses ~**3–4 cm beneath segment IV** (formerly the "quadrate lobe")
- Embraced in a peritoneal sheath at the upper gastrohepatic ligament
- Separated from segment IV's undersurface by connective tissue = the **hilar plate**
- This prolongation turns anteriorly/caudally within the umbilical fissure:
  - Branches to **segment II** first
  - Then **segment III**
  - **Recurrent "feedback vessels"** to segment IV
- Beneath segment IV: pedicle = left portal vein branch + left hepatic duct, joined at the umbilical fissure base by the **left hepatic artery branch**

## Figure 2.7 — Sonographic Portal Vein Bifurcation

- **A**: Transverse sonogram at the portal vein bifurcation level
  - **MPV** (main portal vein) bifurcates into **LPV** and **RPV**
  - **RPV** bifurcates quickly into **RAPV** (right anterior) and **RPPV** (right posterior)
  - **LPV** has a longer horizontal course in the hilar plate
  - **IVC** seen posteriorly
- **B**: Coronal CT angioportography — right hepatic vein and portal vein; anterior/posterior RPV branches arise directly and separately from the main trunk

## Figure 2.8 — Left Portal Vein Branching Pattern

- Transverse sonogram showing **left portal vein (P)** branching pattern
- Courses **horizontally** into the **umbilical fissure**
- **Umbilical portion (U)** of the left portal vein gives branches to **segments 2, 3, 4**
- Left hepatic vein (arrow) and IVC also shown

## Figure 2.9 — CT of Portal Vein Bifurcation

- Contrast-enhanced CT image
- **L** = left portal vein
- **R** = right portal vein
- **RA** = right anterior portal vein
- **RP** = right posterior portal vein
- Demonstrates the typical hilar branching pattern in axial cross-section

## Segment IVa/IVb and Segment I (Caudate) Subdivisions

- Hilar pedicle branching follows a **remarkably symmetric pattern** (Scheele, 1994)
- Allows separation of **segment IV** into:
  - **Segment IVa** (superior)
  - **Segment IVb** (inferior)
- This mimics the segment **V / VIII** relationship on the right
- The **umbilical vein** drains at least parts of segment IVb **after ligation of the middle hepatic vein** — clinically important in segmental resections

## Section 4: The Caudate Lobe (Segment I)

## Caudate Lobe — Overview

- Segment I = **dorsal portion** of liver, lying posteriorly, **embracing the retrohepatic IVC** (Figs 2.10, 2.11)
- Intimately related to several major vascular structures:
  - On the left: between IVC (posterior), left portal triad (inferior), IVC + MHV/LHV (superior) — Fig 2.12
  - Right portion: usually quite **small**, variable in size
- Anterior surface covered by posterior surface of **segment IV**
  - Limit = oblique plane from left portal vein → left hepatic vein
- Adjacent to the recently described **segment IX** (lies between caudate and segment XIII) — authors consider segment IX of **little practical clinical significance**

## Figure 2.10 — CT of Caudate Lobe Relations

- Contrast-enhanced CT scan
- Shows the **intimate relationship** of:
  - Caudate lobe (arrow)
  - IVC
  - Portal vein (p)
  - Aorta (a)

## Figure 2.11 — Caudate Lobe Topography

- Main bulk of segment I (dark area) lies **left of the IVC**; left/inferior margins free in the lesser omental bursa
- Gastrohepatic (lesser) omentum separates the left caudate portion from segments II/III, passing between them to attach to the **ligamentum venosum**
- Left portion of caudate inferiorly traverses **right** between LPV and IVC = **caudate process**, fusing with the right lobe
- Note position of the **MHV**

## Figure 2.12 — Caudate Lobe Rotated View

- Caudate lobe (shaded) + segments II/III, rotated to patient's right
- Left caudate portion linked superiorly by a deep anterior portion embedded under the **MHV**
- Reaches inferiorly to the posterior hilar margin, fuses anterolaterally to IVC on the right with **segments VI and VII**
- Major blood supply: **left branch of LPV + left hepatic artery**, near umbilical fissure base
- Hepatic veins (MHV, LHV) are short, draining caudate directly into anterior/left IVC

## Caudate Lobe — Vascular Supply Pattern

- Supplied and drained by tributaries from **both** right and left portal triads
- **Right portion** (incl. caudate process): portal supply predominantly from **right portal vein** / main portal vein bifurcation
- **Left portion**: portal supply almost exclusively from **left branch** of portal vein
- Arterial supply / biliary drainage follows the same right/left pattern (right posterior sectional vessels vs. left main vessels)
- **Hepatic venous drainage is UNIQUE**: caudate is the **only segment** that drains **directly into the IVC**
  - Can drain into the **posterior** IVC aspect if a retrocaval caudate component is present

## The "Ligament of the Vena Cava" Revisited

- Posterior edge of the caudate (left side) typically has a fibrous component
- Fans out, attaches lightly to the diaphragmatic crura
- Extends posteriorly behind the IVC to link with a fibrous extension from **segment VII** = **venal caval ligament**
- In **up to 50%** of patients: this ligament is replaced (partially/wholly) by hepatic tissue
  - Caudate may **completely encircle the IVC** and contact segment VII on the right
  - A significant **retrocaval component** may prevent a left-sided approach to the caudate veins

## The Caudate's Papillary Process

- Caudal margin of the caudate lobe can show a **papillary projection**
- May attach to the rest of the lobe via a narrow connection
- **Bulky in 27% of cases**
- Can be **mistaken for an enlarged lymph node on CT** — important diagnostic pitfall (Fig 2.13)

## Summary of Liver Functional Anatomy

1. Liver divided into **two hemilivers** by the main hepatic scissura (middle hepatic vein)
2. **Left liver** → two sections: left lateral (II, III) and left medial (IV) — Brisbane 2000
3. **Right liver** → anterior section (V, VIII) and posterior section (VI, VII)
4. **Segment I (caudate)**: lies posteriorly, embraces IVC; intraparenchymal anterior surface abuts segment IV posterior surface; merges with segments VI/VII on the right

## Figure 2.14 — Hepatic Segmental Anatomy on CT

- Three axial CT levels demonstrate segmental boundaries:
  - **A** — Level of the hepatic veins: segments I, II, IVa, VII, VIII visible
  - **B** — Level of portal vein bifurcation: segments I, III, IVb, V, VI visible
  - **C** — Below the hepatic hilus: segments I, III, IVb, V, VI visible
- Demonstrates how segmental boundaries shift at different axial levels — essential for radiologic localization of lesions

## Section 5: Intrahepatic Bile Duct Anatomy

## Intrahepatic Bile Ducts — General Principles

- **Right and left livers** drained by right and left hepatic ducts
- **Caudate lobe** drained by several ducts joining **both** right and left hepatic ducts
- Intrahepatic ducts = tributaries of corresponding hepatic ducts, forming part of major portal triads
- Bile ducts penetrate liver, **invaginating Glisson's capsule** at the hilum
- **Bile ducts** usually lie **above** corresponding portal branches
- **Hepatic arterial branches** sit **inferior** to the veins
- Convergence at the liver hilum → **common hepatic duct**
- Umbilical fissure divides the left liver (between segments III and IV) — may be bridged by a tongue of liver tissue
- **Ligamentum teres** passes through the umbilical fissure to join the **left portal vein branch**

## Left Hepatic Duct — Drainage Pattern (Fig 2.15)

- Drains **segments II, III, and IV** (the left liver)
- The duct draining **segment III** lies slightly behind the **left horn of the umbilical recess**
- Joined by the tributary from **segment IVb** → forms the left duct
- Similarly joined by ducts of **segment II** and **segment IVa** (where the LPV turns forward/caudally)
- Left hepatic duct traverses beneath the left liver, at the base of segment IV
  - Just above/behind the LPV
  - Crosses the anterior LPV edge
  - Joins the right hepatic duct → **hepatic ductal confluence**
- Receives a few small branches from segment IV in its transverse portion

## Right Hepatic Duct — Drainage Pattern (Fig 2.16)

- Drains **segments V, VI, VII, VIII**
- Arises from junction of **two main sectional duct tributaries**, each with corresponding vein and artery:
  - **Right posterior sectional duct**: nearly horizontal course; confluence of segments VI + VII ducts
  - **Right anterior sectional duct**: confluence of segments V + VIII ducts; main trunk lies left of the right anterior sectional portal vein branch (which ascends)
- Junction of these two channels usually occurs **above the right portal vein branch**
- Right hepatic duct is **short**, joins the left hepatic duct → confluence in front of the right portal vein = **common hepatic duct**

## Figure 2.16 — Right Liver Biliary/Vascular Anatomy and a Key Variant

- **A**: Biliary and vascular anatomy of the right liver
  - Horizontal course = **posterior sectional duct**
  - Vertical course = **anterior sectional duct**
- **B**: Trans-tubal cholangiogram — a **common normal variant**
  - **Right posterior sectional duct drains into the left hepatic duct**
  - The posterior duct lies **anterior** to the (expected) posterior sectional duct
  - Frequently, the posterior duct passes **posteriorly** to the anterior sectional pedicle

## Caudate Lobe Biliary Drainage — Statistics

- The caudate lobe has its **own biliary drainage** (Healey & Schroy)
- Divided into: right portion, left portion, and caudate process
- **44%** of individuals: **three separate ducts** drain the three parts
- **26%**: a common duct between right caudate portion + caudate process, plus an independent duct for the left part
- **Drainage destination**:
  - **78%** → right AND left hepatic ducts
  - **15%** → left hepatic ductal system **only**
  - **~7%** → right hepatic system only

## Section 6: Extrahepatic Biliary Anatomy

## Extrahepatic Bile Ducts — Confluence

- Extrahepatic bile ducts = extrahepatic segments of **right and left hepatic ducts** → join to form the **biliary confluence**
- Confluence occurs **right of the hilar fissure**, **anterior** to the portal venous bifurcation, **overlying the origin of the right portal vein branch**
- **Right duct**: short extrahepatic course
- **Left duct**: much **longer** extrahepatic course
- Biliary confluence separated from posterior segment **IVB** by the **hilar plate**

Key teaching points: the bile duct confluence sits **anterior** to the right portal vein branch; the **cystic artery courses posteriorly** behind the common hepatic duct; note the gallbladder neck's relation to the right hepatic artery branch.

## Figure 2.18 — ERCP

- Endoscopic retrograde choledochopancreatogram (ERCP)
- Demonstrates:
  - **Pancreatic duct** (arrow)
  - **Gallbladder**
  - **Biliary tree**
- Classic combined cholangio-pancreatographic view used diagnostically and therapeutically

## Figure 2.19 — The Plate System

The **plate system** = fusion of connective tissue (enclosing biliary/vascular elements) with Glisson's capsule:

- **A — Cystic plate**: above the gallbladder
- **B — Hilar plate**: above the biliary confluence, at the base of segment IV
- **C — Umbilical plate**: above the umbilical portion of the portal vein

Large curving arrows = planes of dissection:

- Cystic plate → during **cholecystectomy**
- Hilar plate → during approaches to the **left hepatic duct**

## Main Bile Duct — Anatomy and Course

- Mean diameter ≈ **6 mm**
- Two portions:
  - **Common hepatic duct** (above the cystic duct)
  - **Common bile duct (CBD)** (below, after cystic duct joins)
- Cystic duct insertion is **variable** — may be as low as the intrapancreatic CBD
- CBD courses **downward anterior to the portal vein**, in the free edge of the lesser omentum
- Closely applied to the **hepatic artery** (runs upward on its left)
- **Right hepatic artery** crosses the main bile duct:
  - **Posteriorly** in most cases
  - **Anteriorly** in ~**20%**

## The Triangle of Calot

- **Cystic artery** (from right hepatic artery branch) may cross the common hepatic duct **anteriorly or posteriorly**
- **Common hepatic duct** = left border of the triangle of Calot
- Original description: cystic duct (below) + cystic artery (above) as the other corners
- **Commonly accepted modern definition**:
  - Upper border = **inferior surface of the right lobe of the liver**
  - Lower border = **cystic duct**
- **Critical surgical relevance**: dissection here is key during cholecystectomy
  - Contains: cystic artery, often the right hepatic artery branch, occasionally a bile duct — must be displayed before cholecystectomy
- If a **replaced/accessory common or right hepatic artery** exists, it usually runs **behind the cystic duct** into the triangle of Calot (Fig 2.21)

## CBD — Retropancreatic Course

- Union between cystic duct and common hepatic duct occurs at **variable levels**
- Lower extrahepatic CBD traverses the **posterior aspect of the pancreas**, running in a groove or tunnel
- Retropancreatic CBD approaches the **2nd portion of the duodenum** obliquely
- Accompanied by the terminal **pancreatic duct of Wirsung**

## Gallbladder — Position and Components

- Reservoir on the undersurface of the **right lobe**, within the **cystic fossa**
- Separated from hepatic parenchyma by the **cystic plate** (connective tissue continuous with the hilar plate)
- Occasionally deeply embedded in the liver; rarely on a mesenteric attachment (→ **volvulus risk**)
- Three parts: **fundus**, **body**, **neck**
- Fundus usually reaches the free liver edge, closely applied to the cystic plate
- **Cystic fossa** = precise anterior landmark to the main liver incisura
- **Neck** angles with the fundus → creates **Hartmann's pouch**
  - May obscure the common hepatic duct → real danger point during cholecystectomy

## Figure 2.20 — Lowering of the Hilar Plate

- **A**: Relationship between posterior segment IV and the biliary confluence
  - Hilar plate (arrow) = fusion of connective tissue + Glisson's capsule
- **B**: Biliary confluence and left hepatic duct exposed by **lifting segment IV upward** after incising Glisson's capsule at its base
  - Used for: dilated bile ducts above iatrogenic strictures or **hilar cholangiocarcinoma**
- **C**: Line of incision for **extensive mobilization of segment IV**
  - Useful for high bile duct strictures, liver atrophy/hypertrophy
  - Combines lifting segment IV + opening umbilical fissure + incising deepest gallbladder fossa

## Cystic Duct — Anatomy

- Arises from the **neck/infundibulum** of the gallbladder, joins the common hepatic duct
- Lumen: ~**1–3 mm**
- Length: variable, depends on union type with common hepatic duct
- Mucosa arranged in spiral folds = **valves of Heister**
- Joins common hepatic duct in its **supraduodenal segment in 80%** of cases
  - May extend down to retroduodenal/retropancreatic area
- **Rarely**: cystic duct may join the **right hepatic duct** or a right hepatic sectional duct directly (Fig 2.24)

## Section 7: Biliary Ductal Anomalies

## Hilar Biliary Confluence Variations — Overview

A "normal" biliary confluence (union of right + left hepatic ducts) occurs in only **72%** of patients (Healey & Schroy; Couinaud)

Key variant patterns:

- **Triple confluence** (right anterior + posterior sectional ducts + left hepatic duct): **12%**
- A right sectional duct joins the **main bile duct directly**: **20%** total
  - Right anterior sectional duct: **16%**
  - Right posterior sectional duct: **4%**

## Hilar Biliary Confluence Variations — Continued

- A right sectional duct joins the **left hepatic duct**: **6%** total
  - Posterior duct: **5%**
  - Anterior duct: **1%**
- **Absence of the hepatic duct confluence**: **3%**
  - Right posterior sectional duct may join the gallbladder neck, or
  - Be entered by the cystic duct (**2%**)

## Figure 2.25 — Main Variations of the Hepatic Duct Confluence (Couinaud)

| Pattern | Description | Frequency |
|---|---|---|
| A | Typical anatomy of the confluence | **57%** |
| B | Triple confluence | **12%** |
| C | Ectopic drainage of a right sectional duct into common hepatic duct (C1 = anterior 16%, C2 = posterior 4%) | **20%** |
| D | Ectopic drainage of a right sectional duct into left hepatic ductal system (D1 = posterior 5%, D2 = anterior 1%) | **6%** |
| E | Absence of the hepatic duct confluence | **3%** |
| F | Absence of right hepatic duct + ectopic right posterior duct into cystic duct | **2%** |

## Intrahepatic Bile Duct Variations — Right Liver

- **Ectopic drainage** rates (Healey & Schroy):
  - **Segment V**: **9%**
  - **Segment VI**: **14%**
  - **Segment VIII**: **20%**
- **Subvesical duct**: described in **20–50%** of cases
  - Sometimes deeply embedded in the cystic plate
  - Joins either common hepatic duct or right hepatic duct
  - Does **not** drain any specific liver territory; never communicates with the gallbladder
  - Not a satellite of an intrahepatic portal vein/hepatic artery branch
  - Injury during cholecystectomy (if cystic plate not preserved) → **postoperative biliary leak**

## Intrahepatic Bile Duct Variations — Left Liver

- "Classic" distribution of the left intrahepatic biliary system: **67%**
- Main variation: **common union between segment III and segment IV ducts** in **25%**
- Only **2%**: segment IV duct joins the common hepatic duct **independently**
- Several anomalies of intrahepatic ducts draining into the gallbladder neck/cystic duct have been described (Fig 2.27)

## Figure 2.26 — Main Variations of the Intrahepatic Ductal System

- **A — Segment V variations**: typical pattern 91%; variants 5%, 4%
- **B — Segment VI variations**: typical pattern 86%; variants 10%, 2%, 2%
- **C — Segment VIII variations**: pattern (a) 80%, pattern (b) 20%
- **D — Segment IV variations**: (a) 67%, (b) 1%, (c) 1%, (d) 25%, (e) 1%, (f) 1%, (g) 4%
- **No variation** described for drainage of **segments II, III, VII**

## Figure 2.24 — T-Tube and ERCP of Low Right Sectional Duct Insertion

- **A**: T-tube cholangiogram — very **low insertion of a right sectional duct** into the common hepatic duct (arrow)
- **B**: ERCP — shows a **low right sectional duct** (large arrow) into which the **cystic duct** is draining (small arrow)
- Described as an **uncommon but important normal variant**

## Figure 2.27 — Ectopic Drainage Into Gallbladder/Cystic Duct

Six described patterns of ectopic intrahepatic duct drainage:

- **A**: Cystic duct drains into the biliary confluence
- **B**: Cystic duct drains into the left hepatic duct (no biliary confluence)
- **C**: Segment VI duct drains into the cystic duct
- **D**: Right posterior (RP) sectional duct drains into the cystic duct
- **E**: Distal RP sectional duct drains into the **neck** of the gallbladder
- **F**: Proximal RP sectional duct drains into the **body** of the gallbladder

## Section 8: Gallbladder and Cystic Duct Anomalies

## Gallbladder Anomalies — Number and Position

- **Agenesis of the gallbladder**: rare, described
- **Bilobar gallbladder**: single cystic duct, two fundi
- **Duplicated gallbladder**: with two cystic ducts
- **Double cystic duct**: draining a unilocular gallbladder
- **Congenital diverticulum** of the gallbladder with a muscular wall
- **Positional anomalies**:
  - **Intrahepatic** position — completely surrounded by normal liver
  - **Left-sided** gallbladder (rare)

## Figure 2.28 — Gallbladder and Cystic Duct Anomalies

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- **A**: Duplicated gallbladder
- **B**: Septum of the gallbladder
- **C**: Diverticulum of the gallbladder
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
- **D**: Variations in cystic ductal anatomy
- **E**: Cystic duct / common hepatic duct union types:
  - (a) Angular — **75%**
  - (b) Parallel — **20%**
  - (c) Spiral — **5%**
:::
:::

## Cystic Duct–Common Hepatic Duct Union — Detail

- **Angular union**: most frequent — **75%** of patients
- **Parallel union**: cystic duct runs parallel to common hepatic duct (**20%**), with connective tissue ensheathing both ducts
- **Spiral union**: cystic duct approaches CBD in a spiral fashion
- **Absence of a cystic duct**: probably an **acquired anomaly**, representing a **cholecystocholedochal fistula**

## Figure 2.22 — Cystic Artery Variations

Eight described variations:

- (a) **Typical course**
- (b) **Double cystic artery**
- (c) Cystic artery crossing **anterior** to main bile duct
- (d) Cystic artery from **right** hepatic artery branch, crossing common hepatic duct anteriorly
- (e) Cystic artery from **left** hepatic artery branch
- (f) Cystic artery from **gastroduodenal artery**
- (g) Cystic artery from **celiac axis**
- (h) Cystic artery from a **replaced right hepatic artery**

## Figure 2.23 — Sonographic Gallbladder Relations

- Longitudinal sonogram
- Demonstrates relationship of:
  - **Liver**
  - **Gallbladder (GB)**
  - **Portal vein (PV)**
  - **IVC**
  - **Hepatic artery** (curved arrow)
  - **Common bile duct** (straight arrow)
- Practical anatomic landmark image for routine ultrasonography

## Section 9: Hepatic Artery Variations

## Hepatic Artery Variations — Frequency

- "Classic" arterial supply pattern present in only ~**60%** of patients
- In ~**25%**: **right hepatic artery** arises partially/completely from the **superior mesenteric artery (SMA)**
- In a similar proportion: **left hepatic artery** may be partially/completely **replaced** by a branch from the **left gastric artery**, coursing through the gastrohepatic omentum to the umbilical fissure base
- Rarely: right or left hepatic arteries originate **independently** from the celiac trunk after a very short common hepatic artery origin
- The **gastroduodenal artery** may originate from the **right hepatic artery** in these variants

## Figure 2.21 — Angiographic Hepatic Artery Variations

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- **A**: Replaced common hepatic artery arising from the **superior mesenteric trunk**
- **B (left)**: Hepatic artery (large arrowhead) arises from the celiac axis; small arrowheads = drainage catheter in bile duct
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
- **B (right)**: **Accessory right hepatic artery** (large arrowhead) from SMA, lateral to CBD catheter
- **C**: Accessory right hepatic artery courses upward **posterolateral to the CBD**, usually behind the **cystic duct (CD)** — occurs in **~25%** of individuals
:::
:::

## Figure 2.37 — Variations Schema and 3D CT Angiography

- Panels A–F: schematic variants where right and/or left hepatic arteries are partially/completely replaced
  - **A, C, E**: right hepatic artery from SMA (~25%)
  - **D, F**: left hepatic artery replaced from left gastric artery (~25%)
- **G**: Multidetector CT angiogram — **accessory right hepatic artery** (arrow) from SMA
- **H**: Multidetector CT angiogram — **replaced left hepatic artery** from left gastric artery
- **I**: Common arterial variant — **hepatic trifurcation**

## Clinical Significance of Replaced Hepatic Arteries

- If common hepatic artery is **entirely replaced** by an artery from the SMA:
  - It passes **posterior, then lateral** to the portal vein as it ascends
  - Lies **posterolateral to the CBD** in the hepatoduodenal ligament
  - **Susceptible to operative injury** if unrecognized — applies to right replaced/accessory hepatic artery too
- Other variations: origin **directly from the aorta**; persistence of a primitive **celiac–SMA embryologic link**
- **Major importance for**: hepatic resection, liver transplantation, hepatic devascularization, intraarterial hepatic infusion device placement, pancreatic head resection

## Section 10: Celiac Axis and Arterial Supply

## Figure 2.34 — Celiac Trunk Branching

- **Celiac trunk**: short, thick artery from the aorta just below the diaphragmatic hiatus
- Divides into: **left gastric, common hepatic, splenic arteries**
- **Inferior phrenic artery**: usually from aorta or splenic artery; occasionally from celiac trunk
- **Left gastric artery**: curves toward stomach, along lesser curve, anastomoses with right gastric artery
- **Splenic artery**: largest celiac branch, tortuous course behind/along the pancreas's upper border to the splenic hilum
  - Usually runs **superior** to the splenic vein
  - **Dangerous variant**: splenic artery running **inferior and behind** the splenic vein near the splenic–mesenteric vein confluence

## Figure 2.34 — Common Hepatic Artery and Branches

- **Common hepatic artery**: enters retroperitoneum, curves right into the lesser omentum above the pancreas
- Approaches CBD on its **left side**, runs **anterior to the portal vein**
- Gives rise to **gastroduodenal artery** (can also originate from right hepatic artery)
  - Supplies anterior/superior/posterior surfaces of the first inch of duodenum
  - Can be **duplicated**; often a small accessory branch toward the pylorus
- **Right gastric artery**: passes left along the lesser curve, anastomoses with left gastric artery
- **Proper hepatic artery** = continuation beyond gastroduodenal + right gastric origins → usually divides into **right and left branches**

## Figure 2.34 — Left and Right Hepatic Artery Branches

- **Left hepatic artery (LH)**: extends vertically toward the umbilical fissure base
  - Gives off the **middle hepatic artery (MH)** → directed toward the right of the umbilical fissure, supplies **segment IV**
  - Further branch → supplies the **caudate lobe**
  - Smaller caudate branches also arise from right hepatic artery
- **Right hepatic artery (RH)**: usually passes **behind** the common hepatic duct, enters the **cystic triangle of Calot**
  - In some cases passes **in front** of the bile duct (important for CBD exposure)
- **Cystic artery**: usually from right hepatic artery, **many variations**

## Figure 2.35 — Pancreatic Arterial Supply

- **Gastroduodenal artery (GDA)**: usually from common hepatic artery (HA), crosses the portal vein (PV) above the pancreas
- **Dorsal pancreatic artery (DP)**: arises from the splenic artery (SA)
- **Superior pancreaticoduodenal arteries (SPDAs)**: from GDA
- **Inferior pancreaticoduodenal arteries (IPDAs)**: from SMA
- SPDAs + IPDAs form **two arcades** (anterior and posterior) along the pancreatic head
- GDA → after giving off the **PDA**, continues as the **right gastroepiploic artery (GEA)**

## GDA as a Surgical Landmark

- **GDA = good landmark** for identifying the portal vein above the pancreas
- **Surgical division of the GDA at its origin** from the common hepatic artery → much greater access to the **anterior surface of the portal vein**
- **Right gastric artery (RGA)**: usually from common HA, just distal to GDA (variable origin)
- GDA commonly divides into a larger **right GEA** and smaller **SPDA**
  - Right GEA: runs forward between duodenum (1st part) and pancreas
  - SPDA: divides into **anterior and posterior branches**
- **Anterior superior PDA**: continues down anterior pancreatic head surface, anastomoses with **IPDA** (from SMA)
- **Posterior superior PDA**: behaves similarly on the posterior surface

## Figure 2.36 — CT of Hepatic Artery and Portal Vein

- Computed tomographic image of the main portal vein
- Demonstrates:
  - **Hepatic artery** (solid arrows) coursing **anterior to portal vein (p)**
  - **Interlobar fissure** (open arrow)
  - **Splenic vein (s)**
  - **Celiac axis (c)**
  - **Aorta (a)**
  - **IVC**

## Section 11: The Portal Vein

## Portal Vein Formation and Course

- Formed **behind the neck of the pancreas** by confluence of the **superior mesenteric vein (SMV)** and **splenic vein (SV)** (Figs 2.38, 2.39)
- Venous drainage of the pancreas runs **parallel to the arterial supply**
- Anterior/posterior and superior/inferior **pancreaticoduodenal veins** drain to portal vein and SMV
- **Left gastric vein** and **inferior mesenteric vein (IMV)** usually drain into the **splenic vein** (can drain directly into portal vein)
- Small splenic tributaries → drain directly to splenic vein

## Figure 2.38 — Portal Vein Formation and Tributaries (Panel A)

- SMV at root of lesser omentum is usually a single trunk (2 or 3 branches may unite as it enters the tunnel beneath the pancreatic neck)
- Joined from the left by the **splenic vein (SV)** → forms the **portal vein (PV)**
- PV emerges from the retroperitoneal upper pancreatic neck border, ascends in the free edge of the lesser omentum
  - Lies **behind** the bile duct and hepatic artery, surrounded by lesser omentum lymphatics/nodes
- Receives the **coronary vein (CV)** — communicates with esophageal venous collaterals (gastric vein + esophageal plexus)
- Sometimes a separate right gastric vein enters PV here
- Superior pancreaticoduodenal vein often enters PV just above the pancreas

## Figure 2.38 — Portal Vein Bifurcation (Panels A, B, C)

- PV bifurcates at the hilum into:
  - Larger **right portal vein (RPV)**
  - Smaller **left portal vein (LPV)**
- **LPV**: courses below the left hepatic duct → enters umbilical fissure with the left hepatic artery → branches to left liver segments **II–IV**
  - Just before entry → gives off a **major caudate vein** (segment I), running posteriorly/laterally to the left
  - Sometimes this vein has 2+ branches
- **RPV**: shorter, divides at the hilar extremity into **RAS** (right anterior sectional) and **RPS** (right posterior sectional) branches, with corresponding arteries and bile ducts
- **B**: division may arise **more proximally**
- **C**: RAS and RPS may arise **independently** from the portal venous trunk

## Figure 2.39 — MRI of Splenoportal Confluence

- Postcontrast T1-weighted 3D gradient-echo coronal MIP (maximum intensity projection)
- Shows:
  - **Splenic vein (s)**
  - **Portal vein (p)**
  - **Superior mesenteric vein (sm)**
- Demonstrates the classic "Y-shaped" splenoportal confluence used for preoperative vascular mapping

## Portal Vein — Relations to the Pancreas

- Anatomic relationship of pancreas to SMV, splenic vein, portal vein = **critical for pancreatic resection**
- **Uncinate process**: extends behind the SMV to a position adjacent to the SMA
- **Access to the portal vein behind the pancreas**: usually from below, elevating the pancreas off the SMV surface (just before it joins splenic vein)
- Branches from the pancreas running **directly posteriorly** into the SMV are **uncommon**
  - Exception: inferior pancreaticoduodenal veins (enter SMV at the inferior pancreatic border)
  - If fixation is seen here → think **inflammatory or neoplastic process**

## Portal Vein Exposure — Surgical Maneuvers

- **Superiorly**: PV identified in the gap between curvature of splenic vein, splenic artery, common hepatic artery, and GDA
- **Division of the GDA** → much greater access to the **superior portal vein surface**
  - Necessary step to **assess tumor involvement of the proximal portal vein**
- If difficulty persists: **division of the CBD** (usually above cystic duct) → excellent access to **right lateral/anterior portal vein surface**
- **SMA approach**: behind the pancreas, above where it's embraced by the uncinate process at its aortic origin → allows dissection of the **most proximal SMA**

## Anatomic Hazards Near the Portal Vein

- Occasionally **middle colic artery** (and other colonic supply vessels) arise from the proximal SMA and **pass through the pancreas** — search for this carefully
  - Division of middle colic artery usually not problematic (colon well-supplied; ischemia uncommon)
- **Head of pancreas relations**:
  - Anteriorly: duodenum
  - Posteriorly: **right renal vein** and **anterior IVC surface**
- **Neck/body of pancreas**: lie atop SMA, splenic vessels, **left renal vein**, and (more laterally) the **left kidney**

## Pancreatic Mobilization — Venous Tributaries to Ligate

- **Right gastroepiploic vein**: commonly drains into the anterior SMV surface at the pancreatic inferior border
  - Can be **involved by tumor**
- **Anterior branch of inferior pancreaticoduodenal vein**: similarly positioned, can be tumor-involved
- **Middle colic vein**: may also join at this point
- **During SMV mobilization**: these vessels are **ligated** to avoid bothersome hemorrhage
- **IVC abnormalities**: uncommon (duplication, left-sided IVC — both rare)

## Section 12: Portal Vein Variants and Anomalies

## Portal Vein Anomalies — Clinical Stakes

- Several variations/rare congenital anomalies are **of major surgical significance** (Figs 2.40–2.43)
- **Critical example**: performing right hepatic resection while dividing what *appears* to be the right portal vein in a patient with **absence of the left portal vein** → **can be FATAL**
- **Agenesis of the right portal vein branch** associated with:
  - Agenesis of the right hemiliver
  - Left liver hypertrophy
  - May coexist with biliary and hepatic venous anomalies → compromises surgical/biliary repair approaches

## Figure 2.40 — Portal Vein Trifurcation Pattern

- Contrast-enhanced CT scan
- Demonstrates a **variant trifurcation pattern**:
  - **L** = left portal vein
  - **M** = main portal vein
  - **RA** = right anterior portal vein
  - **RP** = right posterior portal vein
- The right anterior and posterior sectoral veins arise as **separate branches directly from the main trunk** — a pattern that can mimic a standard bifurcation if not carefully assessed

## Figure 2.41 — Rare Portal Vein Positional Anomalies

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**A**

- Portal vein **anterior to the head of the pancreas and duodenum** may occur in an **abnormal position**
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**B & C**

- **B**: Rare anomaly — **entrance of the portal vein into the IVC**
- **C**: Very rare — **entrance of a pulmonary vein into the portal vein**
:::
:::

## Figure 2.42 — Congenital Absence of the Left Portal Vein Branch

- As described by **Couinaud**
- The **right portal vein branch** courses through the right lobe, supplying it
- It then **curves within the liver substance** to also supply the **left lobe**
- In these instances, the left lobe is **usually smaller than normal**
- This is the exact anomaly responsible for the "fatal right hepatectomy" scenario described earlier

## Figure 2.43 — Caroli's Disease with Absent Left Portal Branch

- CT scan in a patient with **Caroli's disease**
- Shows a **large right portal trunk**
- **Left branch of the portal vein is absent**
- Findings **confirmed at operation** — patient underwent **left hepatic lobectomy**
- Demonstrates real-world correlation of the Fig 2.42 schematic anomaly with clinical imaging

## Section 13: The Pancreas — Gross Anatomy

## Pancreas — Overview

- A **posteriorly situated retroperitoneal organ**, lying **transversely**
- Composed of: **head, neck, body, tail**
- **Head**: encompassed by the duodenum
- **Tail**: rests in the **splenic hilum**
- **Uncinate process**: inferior portion of the head, intimately related to **SMV and SMA**
- **Posteriorly related to**: IVC, aorta, left renal vein, left kidney, spleen
- Portion **lateral to the portal vein** averages **56.4%** of total pancreatic weight
- Pancreatic capsule loosely attached, **contiguous with the anterior mesocolon layer** — can be dissected in continuity if necessary
- Mesenteric attachments to the pancreas tend to be **contiguous**

## Figure 2.44 — MRI and CT of Normal Pancreatic Anatomy

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**A — MRI**

- Oblique axial reconstruction, T1-weighted 3D gradient-echo
- Shows: **aorta (a)**, **IVC (i)**, **CBD** (arrow), **SMV at splenoportal confluence (v)**, **SMA** (arrowhead), **left renal vein (r)**
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**B — CT**

- Postcontrast CT at pancreatic level
- Shows: **A** (aorta), **a** (SMA), **D** (duodenum), **IVC**, **S** (stomach), **v** (SMV)
- Long arrow = CBD; short arrow = inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery; open arrow = GDA
:::
:::

## Figure 2.45 — The Uncinate Process

- Head of the pancreas is **globular**, with the **uncinate process** extension
- Curves **behind the superior mesenteric vessels**
- Three patterns (a, b, c) — **all commonly seen**:
  - (a) May end before embracing the SMV
  - (b, c) May pass completely behind, between the aorta and the left of the SMA
- **Posteriorly**: head of pancreas in juxtaposition to IVC at the level of left/right renal vein entry
- **Neck**: forms in front of the SMV–splenic vein confluence, joins the **body** (forms the narrowing **tail**)

## Figure 2.45 — CBD Position Within the Pancreas

- **CBD** passes through the pancreas:
  - Either **directly within the gland substance**, OR
  - Initially within a **posterior groove**
- Three positional variants are illustrated (left, middle, right panels) showing the CBD's location relative to the pancreatic head outline

## Figure 2.45 — Duct of Wirsung and Duct of Santorini

- **Duct of Wirsung**: courses **left → right** within the pancreas, curves downward toward the CBD
  - Runs **parallel but separate** from the CBD, divided by the **transampullary septum**
  - Enters duodenum **7–10 cm distal to the pylorus**, at the **papilla of Vater**, after traversing the **sphincter of Oddi**
- **Duct of Santorini** (accessory duct): runs more proximally in the pancreatic head, usually terminates at an **accessory papilla**
- Multiple variations depending on duct of Santorini development:
  - **(i)**: Direct communication with the main duct
  - **(ii)**: Duplicate/separate systems = **pancreas divisum**
- **Duct of Santorini** drains body + tail; **Duct of Wirsung** drains head + uncinate process

## Section 14: Pancreatic Duct Anatomy and Variants

## The Sphincter of Oddi (Fig 2.47)

- Thoroughly studied structure (Boyden 1957; Delmont 1979)
- Consists of a **unique cluster of smooth muscle fibers** distinguishable from adjacent duodenal wall smooth muscle
- **Papilla of Vater**: small nipple-like structure at CBD termination, protruding into the duodenal lumen
  - Marked by a **longitudinal fold of duodenal mucosa**
- Components illustrated:
  - (a) Notch
  - (b) Biliary sphincter
  - (c) Transampullary septum
  - (d) Pancreatic sphincter
  - (e) Membranous septum of Boyden
  - (f) Common sphincter
  - (g) Smooth muscle of duodenal wall

## Duct of Wirsung — Termination Patterns

- Runs downward, **parallel to the CBD** for approximately **2 cm**
- Joins the CBD **within the sphincter segment** in **70–85%** of patients
- Enters the duodenum **independently** in **10–13%** of patients
- **Replaced by the duct of Santorini** in **2%** of patients

## Pancreas Divisum

- **Rarely**: duct of Santorini and duct of Wirsung remain **completely separate** = **pancreas divisum**
- Important congenital anatomic variant, relevant to recurrent pancreatitis and ERCP cannulation strategy

## Figure 2.48 — MRCP Findings

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**A**

- MRCP, T2-weighted coronal image at the ampulla level
- Shows duodenum (D), pancreatic head with CBD (curved arrow) and pancreatic duct (straight arrow)
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**B — Pancreas Divisum**

- Anterior projection
- **Duct of Santorini** (vertical arrow) lies between the duodenum and the duct of Wirsung (angled arrow), shown as **two separate ducts**
- Santorini drains mainly neck/body; Wirsung drains mainly the uncinate portion of the head
:::
:::

## Annular Pancreas

- Development of a **ring of pancreatic tissue** that surrounds (often embraces) the duodenum
- May contain a **large duct**; can be firmly affixed to duodenal musculature
- Duodenum beneath this annulus is **often stenosed**
- Dividing the ring **does NOT always relieve chronic duodenal obstruction**
- Common treatment: **duodenojejunostomy** to relieve strictures caused by the annulus

- **Transverse mesocolon** arises from the lower pancreatic border, envelops the **middle colic vessels** as they arise from the superior mesenteric vessels beneath the pancreatic neck

## Section 15: Bile Duct Blood Supply

## Bile Duct — Three Segments and Their Supply

The bile duct is divided into **three segments**:

1. **Hilar**
2. **Supraduodenal**
3. **Retropancreatic**

- **Supraduodenal duct** blood supply: essentially **axial** (Fig 2.29; Northover & Terblanche, 1979)
- Sources: superior pancreaticoduodenal artery, right hepatic artery branch, cystic artery, gastroduodenal artery, retroduodenal artery
- On average: **8 small arteries**, each ~**0.3 mm** diameter, supply the supraduodenal duct

## The 3 O'Clock and 9 O'Clock Arteries

- The **most important** supraduodenal duct vessels run along the **lateral and medial borders** of the duct
- Named the **3 o'clock** and **9 o'clock arteries**
- Of all vessels vascularizing the supraduodenal duct:
  - **60%** run **upward** from the major inferior vessels
  - **38%** run **downward**, originating from the right hepatic artery branch and other vessels
  - Only **2%** are **non-axial** — arising directly from the main hepatic artery trunk as it courses parallel to the biliary channel

## Hilar and Retropancreatic Duct Blood Supply

- **Hilar ducts**: receive a **copious arterial supply** from surrounding vessels
  - Form a **rich network** on the duct surface, continuous with the supraduodenal plexus
- **Retropancreatic CBD**: blood supply from the **retroduodenal artery**
  - Provides multiple small vessels forming a **mural plexus** around the duct

## Figure 2.29 — Bile Duct Blood Supply Diagram

- Demonstrates the **axial arrangement** of supraduodenal bile duct vasculature
- Shows the **rich network** enclosing right and left hepatic ducts
- Labeled vessels:
  - (a) Right hepatic artery branch
  - (b) **9 o'clock artery**
  - (c) Retroduodenal artery
  - (d) Left hepatic artery branch
  - (e) Hepatic artery
  - (f) **3 o'clock artery**
  - (g) Common hepatic artery
  - (h) Gastroduodenal artery

## Bile Duct Venous Drainage

- Veins draining the bile ducts are **satellites of the corresponding arteries**
- Drain into **3 o'clock and 9 o'clock veins** along the common biliary channel borders
- **Gallbladder-draining veins**: empty into **this venous system**, NOT directly into the portal vein
- The biliary tree appears to have its **own portal venous pathway** to the liver — clinically important concept

## Section 16: Anatomy of Biliary Exposure

## The Plate System — Surgical Application

- Fusion of Glisson's capsule with connective tissue sheaths around biliary/vascular elements at the liver's inferior surface = the **plate system**
- Components:
  - **Hilar plate** — above the biliary confluence
  - **Cystic plate** — related to the gallbladder
  - **Umbilical plate** — above the umbilical portion of the left portal vein
- **Hepp and Couinaud (1956)** technique: lift segment IV upward + incise Glisson's capsule at its base → good exposure of hilar structures = **"lowering of the hilar plate"**
- Safe in **99%** of cases — major vascular interposition between hilar plate and liver's inferior aspect occurs in only **1%** (tiny venules are common, however)

## Lowering of the Hilar Plate — Indications and Limits

- **Particularly valuable** for exposing the **extrahepatic left hepatic duct** (long course beneath segment IV)
- **Less effective** for the extrahepatic **right duct** or its secondary branches (these are short)
- **Major importance**: identification of **proximal biliary mucosa** during bile duct repair after injury
- Basic technique:
  1. Incise at the posterior edge of segment IV (where Glisson's capsule attaches to the hilar plate)
  2. Separate the hilar plate's upper surface from hepatic parenchyma
  3. Lift segment IV upward → displays the hepatic duct convergence (**always extrahepatic**)
  4. Bile duct incision → allows a **mucosa-to-mucosa anastomosis**

## When Standard Hilar Approach Is Hazardous

- Rarely hazardous, especially when:
  - Anatomic deformity from **atrophy or hypertrophy** of liver lobes
  - A **very deep hilum** displaced upward and rotated laterally
- **Alternative**: simultaneous opening of:
  - The **deepest portion of the gallbladder fossa**
  - The **umbilical fissure**
- → good exposure of the biliary confluence (especially the right hepatic duct) **without full hepatotomy**

## Figure 2.20 — Recap of Hilar Plate Exposure Steps

- Reinforces the **A → B → C** sequence:
  - **A**: hilar plate anatomy at segment IV
  - **B**: confluence and left hepatic duct exposed by lifting segment IV
  - **C**: incision lines for extensive segment IV mobilization (umbilical fissure + gallbladder fossa)
- Image **B** is credited to **Hepp J, Couinaud C. Presse Med. 1956;64:947–948**

## Umbilical Fissure / Segment III (Ligamentum Teres) Approach

- The **round ligament** (remnant of obliterated umbilical vein) runs through the umbilical fissure to connect with the **left portal vein branch**
- Sometimes deeply embedded in the umbilical fissure
- At the junction of the round ligament and LPV termination: elongations containing left portal system elements course into the liver
- **Bile ducts of the left lobe** (Figs 2.30, 2.31A):
  - Located **above** the LPV branch
  - Lie **behind** these vascular elongations
  - Corresponding **artery** sits **below** the vein

## Segment III Duct — Exposure Technique

- Dissection of the round ligament on its **left side** + division of **1–2 vascular elongations of segment III**
- → displays the pedicle/anterior branch of the **segment III duct** (Fig 2.32)
- **In biliary obstruction with intrahepatic dilation**: a dilated segment III duct is generally **easily located above the LPV branch**
- **Preferred technique**: split normal liver tissue **just left of the umbilical fissure** to widen it
  - → access to the ductal system **without** dividing portal blood supply elements to segment III

## Figure 2.30 — Left Liver Biliary/Vascular Anatomy

- Demonstrates the **biliary and vascular anatomy of the left liver**
- Note: location of the **segment III duct above its corresponding vein**
- The **anterior branch of the segment IV duct** is **not represented** in this figure

## Section 17: Right Hepatic Duct Exposure & Hepatic Trisectionectomy Anatomy

## Surgical Approaches to the Right Hepatic Biliary System

- **Right intrahepatic ductal system exposure** is **much more hazardous and imprecise** than the left
  - Due to lack of precise anatomic landmarks
- In some hilar cholangiocarcinoma cases, a planned partial hepatectomy or segment III duct bypass may **seem impossible**
- **Option**: intrahepatic right ductal system drainage
- **Anatomic basis**: the anterior sectional duct and its branches run **on the left side** of the corresponding portal vein

## Figure 2.33 — Anterior Sectional Duct Approach

- **A**: If necessary, liver substance opened through a short distance along the line of the **right anterior sectional pedicle**
- The portion of the right portal vein opened through a short distance; **anterior sectional duct displayed on the left aspect** of the vein
- Dilated duct opened **longitudinally**, sewn to a **Roux-en-Y jejunal loop**
- **B**: Duct displayed **anterior and to the left** of the corresponding vein
  - Can be facilitated by a **posterior pedicular approach** (Launois technique)
- Technique is **rarely used** but may be valuable in selected cases
- **Preferred alternative**: encircle/expose right-sided pedicles via the standard right-sided liver resection technique

## Exposure of Bile Ducts by Liver Resection

- A segment of the **left lobe** may be amputated to expose **segment II or III ducts**
- A similar procedure may follow removal of the **inferior tip of the right lobe**
- **Segment IV resection** may be carried out to effect exposure of the **biliary confluence**
- This represents a **simple extension** of segment IV mobilization (after opening the principal scissura and umbilical fissure, as previously described)

## Section 18: Lymphatic Drainage and Nerve Supply

## Lymphatic Drainage — Liver and Gallbladder

- **Liver and gallbladder** drain mainly to:
  - **Hepatoduodenal nodes** at the hilus
  - Nodes **along the hepatic artery and portal vein**
- **Gallbladder**: drains partly to the liver, but also via the **cystic node** to:
  - Nodes of the **hepatoduodenal ligament**
  - **Suprapancreatic nodes**

## Lymphatic Drainage — Pancreas

- Predominantly to nodes lying **in juxtaposition to the arteries and veins**
- **Numerous nodes (i)** lie along the **SMV** at the pancreatic borders:
  - Drain back to **splenic hilar nodes**
  - Along the pancreatic superior border → **superior pancreatic nodes**
  - → **celiac trunk** and nodes at the **common hepatic artery base**
- A **large node** commonly lodges at the superior pancreatic border / right side of the common hepatic artery
  - Often needs **dissection and elevation** to access the anterior portal vein surface
  - Removal **improves access**, as does division of the GDA
- **Posterior pancreaticoduodenal nodes (ii)**: lie along the **posterior pancreaticoduodenal arterial arcade**

## Nerve Supply to the Liver and Pancreas

- Supply derives from branches of the **celiac ganglion**
- Composed of:
  - **Sympathetic** elements
  - **Parasympathetic** elements
- Distribution is **mainly in association with major arteries**

## Figure 2.50 — Autonomic Innervation

- Diagram shows distribution of **sympathetic and parasympathetic nerves** to the liver and pancreas from the **celiac ganglion**
- Key labeled structures:
  - **Vagal nerves** (parasympathetic input)
  - **Splanchnic nerves** (sympathetic input)
  - **Celiac ganglion** (central relay)
- Nerve fibers travel predominantly **along the course of the major arteries** supplying the liver and pancreas

## Closing Summary

## Key Take-Home Points

- The liver is functionally divided by **hepatic vein-containing scissurae** into 8 Couinaud segments / 4 Brisbane sections per hemiliver
- The **caudate lobe (segment I)** is anatomically and functionally unique — bilateral portal supply, bilateral biliary drainage, and **direct IVC venous drainage**
- **Biliary, arterial, and portal venous anomalies are common** (only ~60–72% follow "classic" patterns) — recognition is essential to avoid catastrophic injury
- The **plate system** (hilar, cystic, umbilical plates) underlies safe biliary exposure techniques
- Pancreatic ductal anatomy (Wirsung/Santorini, pancreas divisum, annular pancreas) has direct clinical relevance to pancreatitis and ERCP
- Vascular relationships of the **portal vein, SMV, splenic vein, and GDA** are central to safe pancreatic and hepatic resection
